[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == {{Japanese clan infobox |name = Moriya clan |crest = Maru ni Hidari Jū no Ji.svg|thumb|130px|Circle with left cross |crest_name = Circle with left cross |honorific_ancestry = [[Kami clan]]
[[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == {{Japanese clan infobox |name = Moriya clan |crest = Maru ni Hidari Jū no Ji.svg|thumb|130px|Circle with left cross |crest_name = Circle with left cross |honorific_ancestry = [[Kami clan]]
[[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == {{Japanese clan infobox |name = Moriya clan |crest = Maru ni Hidari Jū no Ji.svg|thumb|130px|Circle with left cross |crest_name = Circle with left cross |honorific_ancestry = [[Kami clan]]
[[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == {{Japanese clan infobox |name = Moriya clan |crest = Maru ni Hidari Jū no Ji.svg|thumb|130px|Circle with left cross |crest_name = Circle with left cross |honorific_ancestry = [[Kami clan]]
[[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命}}, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == {{Japanese clan infobox |name = Moriya clan |crest = Maru ni Hidari Jū no Ji.svg|thumb|130px|Circle with left cross |crest_name = Circle with left cross |honorific_ancestry = [[Kami clan]]
[[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神|1=Moritaku-no-Kami}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫|1=Tamatsuhime}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikato no Kami}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神|1=Moritaku-no-Kami}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫|1=Tamatsuhime}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikatō-no-Kami}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (burial mound) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == {{Japanese clan infobox |name = Moriya clan |crest = Maru ni Hidari Jū no Ji.svg|thumb|130px|Circle with left cross |crest_name = Circle with left cross |honorific_ancestry = [[Kami clan]]
[[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神|1=Moritaku-no-Kami}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫|1=Tamatsuhime}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikatō-no-Kami}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (Kofun) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Kamibe clan]]
[[Mononobe clan]]? |founder = {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} or {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}}
Mononobe lineage, {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋}} branch (see below) |type = [[Shinto priest clan]]
[[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神|1=Moritaku-no-Kami}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫|1=Tamatsuhime}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikatō-no-Kami}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (Kofun) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == [[Samurai clan]] |origin = [[Shinano Province]], [[Suwa District, Nagano|Suwa District]] |location = Shinano Province, Suwa District |notable_members = [[Moriya Yoritane]] }} '''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials. == Origins == [[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}} to Yagushi no Kami).]] The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神|1=Moritaku-no-Kami}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫|1=Tamatsuhime}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikatō-no-Kami}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (Kofun) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == According to family tradition, they are descendants of {{ill|Moreya no Kami|ja|洩矢神|12=draft}}, a terrestrial deity who opposed {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神|12=draft}} (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto|12=draft}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikatō-no-Kami|12=draft}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: {{ill|Morotaku no Kami|ja|守宅神|1=Moritaku-no-Kami}} and {{ill|Tamamoru Hime|ja|多満留姫|1=Tamatsuhime}}. Tamamoru Hime married {{ill|Izuhaya no Mikoto|ja|出早雄命|1=Izuhayao-no-Mikoto}} , a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered {{ill|Chikatsu no Kami|ja|千鹿頭神|1=Chikatō-no-Kami}}, who became Moreya's ritual successor.{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336. Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern {{ill|Kanda, Matsumoto|ja|神田 (松本市)}}) and married {{ill|Urakohime no Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命}}. This lineage continued through their grandson, {{ill|Kodamahiko no Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命}}. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants. == Religious and Political Role == [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya’s son, Takemaro.]] The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}}. == Cultural and Historical Legacy == === Fune Kofun === The {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (Kofun) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}} === Suwa Faith === The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history. == Notable Members == * [[Moriya Yoritane]]: A prominent ''jinchōkan'' during the Sengoku period. == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Suwa Grand Shrine|ja|諏訪大社|1=Suwa-taisha}} * {{ill|Fune Kofun|ja|フネ古墳}} * {{ill|Mishaguji|ja|ミシャグジ}} {{Suwa Faith}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Moriya clan]] [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Shinano Province]] [[Category:Shinto priest clans]] [[Category:Suwa faith]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] }} [[sn:Moriya clan]] [[ja:守矢氏]] [[Category:Ja import oversized]]
